title: Lior and the Visitor
premise: Mara Ashgrove, a pest controller who prides himself on never believing in anything he can't spray, trap, or bill for, is called to the Holloway house where something leaves fingerprints on the inside of sealed windows. When every mirror begins reflecting the room one second late, Mara realizes the delay is a countdown — and that the 'visitor' is a drowned child, Lior, whose death the household sang about and then buried from memory. The house demands someone learn the song's final verse without singing along, because the verse names the person who let Lior die. As the mirrors close their one-second gap, Mara must choose between protecting his client — the woman who watched Lior drown and paid everyone to forget — and giving the visitor the truth it has waited thirty years to hear. In the end Mara speaks the verse aloud as testimony rather than song, freeing Lior but shattering the household, and walks out of a house whose mirrors now show only empty rooms.
about_author: Ansel Pemberton is the pen name of a former building inspector who spent fifteen years crawling through other people's basements and swears half of what he saw down there doesn't have an explanation. He writes horror about houses that remember, and lives in a rented flat with no mirrors in the bathroom.

chapters.title: Fingerprints on the Inside
chapters.summary: Mara Ashgrove takes a routine call to the Holloway house: something leaving small handprints on the inside of sealed upstairs windows. Told in Mara's dry, skeptical POV, he inspects, finds nothing, and bills accordingly. The emotional beat is smug professional confidence — the reader sees the first crack when he notices the prints are fresh and the window was painted shut decades ago.

chapters.title: The Client Who Won't Look Up
chapters.summary: POV Mara. He returns to collect payment and meets Edith Holloway, who keeps her eyes on the floor and pays double to make him stop coming. Her adult son Corin watches Mara leave and mouths 'help us.' The beat is unease: money offered too eagerly, a house too quiet, a woman rehearsing her own denial.

chapters.title: One Second Late
chapters.summary: POV Mara, back home. His bathroom mirror reflects him raising a coffee cup one full second after he does it. He tests it for hours, timing it against his phone camera, until the lag shrinks to half a second. The beat shifts from skepticism to dread — the skeptic's toolkit becomes an instrument of terror.

chapters.title: A Song Half-Remembered
chapters.summary: POV Edith, decades earlier: a summer house full of cousins, a boy named Lior who couldn't swim, and a skipping song the children sang by the pond. Edith remembers singing it, remembers stopping mid-verse, remembers never asking why. The beat is guilty nostalgia — memory presented as innocence that isn't.

chapters.title: Called Back
chapters.summary: POV Mara. Edith calls at 3 a.m.: the mirrors are all wrong, please come, bring whatever you brought last time. Mara arrives to find every reflective surface in the house running a second behind, including a dark television and a polished banister. Corin begs him to stay. The beat is reluctant entanglement — the pest controller hired for ghosts he doesn't believe in.

chapters.title: What the Delay Hides
chapters.summary: POV Mara. He experiments: stand before a mirror long enough and the reflection stops copying you and starts doing something else — a small figure standing behind your shoulder, gone when you turn. He finds wet footprints leading from the bathroom to the pond-side nursery. Beat: the skeptic starts keeping notes like a believer.

chapters.title: Corin's Version
chapters.summary: POV Corin. He tells Mara about his childhood: Lior was his cousin, drowned in the pond while the adults were inside, and afterward the family simply stopped saying his name. Corin was six; he's been hearing the song through the walls ever since. Beat: grief weaponized into silence, and the first alliance between Mara and someone inside the house.

chapters.title: Edith Denies Everything
chapters.summary: POV Edith, present day. Confronted by Mara, she insists Lior never existed, produces no photographs, and threatens legal action. Alone, she opens a locked drawer, touches a child's shoe, and closes it again. Beat: loyalty curdling into complicity — she protected the family name so long she's forgotten which lie came first.

chapters.title: The Verse That Isn't Sung
chapters.summary: POV Mara. Researching local archives, he finds the skipping song printed in a 1970s schoolbook — with a final verse marked 'omitted from local versions.' The verse names a watcher who saw a child go under and walked away. Beat: the horror acquires grammar; the house isn't haunting, it's waiting for a witness.

chapters.title: Singing Along
chapters.summary: POV Corin. Corin tries to sing the recovered verse aloud to end it, and the mirrors snap into perfect sync — and then begin showing rooms that don't exist, filling with water. Something nearly takes him. Beat: the rule revealed — the verse must be known, not sung; performance feeds the visitor, testimony frees it.

chapters.title: Wet Carpets Rising
chapters.summary: POV Mara. The house begins flooding from the inside: damp climbing the wallpaper, the pond sound audible in every room, mirrors now lagging two seconds and gaining. Mara realizes the one-second gap is a fuse. Beat: escalating siege, the professional's calm cracking into genuine fear.

chapters.title: The Neighbor Who Left
chapters.summary: POV Mara interviews Dora, an elderly former neighbor, who recalls the drowning and the hush-money: Edith's father paid several families to move away and forget. She remembers who else was at the pond that day — and refuses to say more, terrified. Beat: justice outside the law taking shape; the cover-up had architects.

chapters.title: Lag Zero
chapters.summary: POV Mara. At dawn the mirrors sync perfectly — and Lior stands in all of them at once, patient, dripping, holding up fingers counting down from ten. Each hour a mirror goes dark permanently. Beat: the deadline made visible; Mara understands he isn't investigating anymore, he's been summoned.

chapters.title: Edith's Confession, Almost
chapters.summary: POV Edith. Cornered by rising water and Mara's questions, Edith admits a boy drowned, admits she was there — then blames her father, the neighbors, the times. The mirrors show her the pond, the sun on the water, a small hand slipping from hers. Beat: the cost of a lifetime's loyal lying made flesh; she breaks but won't yet speak.

chapters.title: Corin Disappears
chapters.summary: POV Mara. Corin ventures toward the nursery to apologize to Lior himself and vanishes; his voice joins the song behind the walls, singing verses he shouldn't know. Mara hears his own childhood hummed back at him in Corin's register. Beat: personal stakes ignite — the house has learned how to take people Mara cares about.

chapters.title: The Pond Under the Floorboards
chapters.summary: POV Mara. He tears up the nursery floor and finds the old well the pond fed, black water rising, Lior's shoe on the lip. In the water's surface — a mirror — he sees the whole household from that day: Edith, fourteen years old, watching, turning away. Beat: the truth located physically beneath the house of lies.

chapters.title: What Edith Saw
chapters.summary: POV Edith, finally unguarded. Full flashback: she dared Lior toward the deep edge, saw him slip, froze, ran inside, and told her father nothing; the silence was her inheritance and then her religion. Beat: the theme lands — loyalty to family versus truth to the dead — and she chooses, at last, to speak.

chapters.title: Learning Without Singing
chapters.summary: POV Mara. With Edith's account complete, Mara memorizes the final verse silently, writing it out, mouthing nothing, while the house floods faster and the last mirrors darken. Corin's voice guides him from behind the wall, correcting each line. Beat: quiet, concentrated terror — the climax approached through stillness and discipline.

chapters.title: Testimony
chapters.summary: POV Mara, climax. Standing at the open well with the water at his knees, Mara recites the verse aloud as witness statement — naming Edith, naming the silence, naming Lior — refusing its rhythm so it cannot become a song. The mirrors shatter outward; the water drains; Lior appears once, un-drowned, and lets go of Corin's hand. Beat: catharsis through truth spoken outside any law but honesty.

chapters.title: After the Water
chapters.summary: POV Corin. The house is ordinary, damaged, drained. Edith, aged visibly overnight, tells Corin everything and asks nothing of him. Neighbors gather at the dried pond bed where small flowers appear by morning. Beat: grief finally allowed to be grief; the family name dies so the boy can live in memory.

chapters.title: Empty Rooms
chapters.summary: POV Mara. Final walkthrough: he repairs nothing, bills nothing, and checks every mirror — they reflect instantly, faithfully, boringly. Only the nursery window still shows, faintly, handprints drying in sunlight. Beat: release with residue; the skeptic leaves believing exactly one thing.

chapters.title: The Song Somewhere Else
chapters.summary: POV Mara, coda. Weeks later, in another town on another job, Mara hears children skipping to a tune he knows — and stops them before the last verse, teaching them instead to end the song with a name said plainly: Lior. They do, and laugh, and run on. Beat: resolution as transmission — justice carried forward gently, and the horror closed by being remembered right.
